div.head: W e propose worst-case response time schedulabili t y analysis f o r fault-tolerant hard real-time systems which takes i n t o account the effects of temporary faults.
div.p: T h e major contribution of our approach is to consider the recovery of tasks running with higher priorities. This characteristic is very useful since faulty tasks certainly have a shorter period of t i m e t o meet their deadlines. D u e to its flexibility and simplicity, the proposed approach provides a n eflectiue schedulability analysis, where system predictability can be fully guaranteed.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The ability to tolerate faults is an extremely desired characteristic for hard real-time systems. Nevertheless, the implementation of such systems is far from being simple. It involves both suitable schedulability analysis, which takes the effects of possible faults into account, and fault tolerance mechanisms, which keep the system computation complying with the specification even in the presence of faults. In other words, tasks that may be performed by the fault tolerance mechanism have to be taken into account by the schedulability analysis.

Due to the required fault tolerance/schedulability analysis synergy and the uncertain nature of faults, most papers published up to date have proposed restrictive and/or ad hoc solutions to the schedulability analysis. As a result, those solutions impair the applicability and flexibility of the analysis. By contrast, a recent approach (3; 13) based on the well known response time analysis (1) has eliminated these drawbacks by not restricting the way that fault tolerance *Supported by CAPES/Brazil under grant: BEX4738/98-0.

is carried out and by assuming realistic fault and task models. In this work we generalise this approach by allowing task recovery to execute with higher priority, which increases the flexibility of the analysis. This can be very useful since, after a fault, tasks certainly have a shorter period of time to meet their deadlines. Indeed, data collected from simulation has illustrated that significant gains in terms of reduction of recovery time may be obtained using our approach.

As in (3), we are concerned in this work only with temporary faults. This kind of fault originates either from some disturbances in the external environment (transient faults) or from the presence of rarely occurring combinations of conditions in respect of the internal state (intermittent faults) (8). Indeed, since temporary faults are usually more frequent than perman e n t faults (12) and the tolerance of permanent faults requires hardware redundancy (which increase dramatically the cost and complexity of its implementation), a system that tolerates temporary faults is usually more cost-effective.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The next section presents the assumed computational model and introduces our notation. Section 3 describes briefly some concepts regarding the use of response time analysis for fault tolerance purposes. The main result of this paper is presented in section 4. Section 5 describes a simple evaluation of our solution based on simulation. Our approach is compared with related work in section 6 . Finally, section 7 offers our conclusion.

div.p: We assume that there is a set I? = ( 7 1 , .. . , 7,) of n tasks, called primary tasks, that must be scheduled by the system in the absence of faults. Any primary task ri in r has a period, Ti, a deadline Di, and a worst-case computation time, Ci (Di 5 Ti). Tasks can be periodic or sporadic. For sporadic tasks the period means the minimum inter-arrival time. Each primary task ri can have mi alternative tasks associated with it, i.e. for all ri there exists yi = { T i , . . . ,7y'} (mi 2 1). This assumption is not a restriction of our model and it is useful since we do not need to include unnecessary details in the description we shall present. Thus we only need to refer to 7i as the worst-case alternative task in case of faults in task ri.

Primary tasks are scheduled according to some fixed priority assignment algorithm (e.g. deadline monotonic), which attributes a distinct priority to each task ~i in r. We consider n different priority levels ( 1 , 2 , . . . , n ) , where 1 and n represent the highest and the lowest priority levels, respectively. Alternative tasks are assumed to execute with the same or higher priorities than their respective primary tasks. We denote the priority of rz and as pr(ri) and pr(7i), respectively. When a primary task, say ~i , and an alternative task, say ?j, are ready to execute at the same priority level we assume that Tj is scheduled first. For the simplicity of notation we define two subsets of r (others will be defined when necessary): hp(i) represents the tasks whose priorities are greater than ~i ' s priority and hpe(i) denotes those tasks whose priorities are greater than or equal to ri's priority (hpe(i) = hp(i) U { r i } ) .

We consider only the occurrence of temporary software faults in a uniprocessor system where recovery techniques such as recovery blocks, exception handling or task re-executions are appropriate (3). When a fault hits a task, say ri, the system must schedule an appropriate alternative task, say 7;

We also assume that there is no cost associated with any scheduling of primary or alternative tasks. Also, we assume that all faults are detected by the system and there is no fault propagation (i.e. faults affect only the executing task). The assumed fault model considers that the fault -k arrival rate is bounded (i.e there is a minimum interval between two consecutive faults). We denote TF as the minimum assumed time between faults. div.p: As we have seen, it would be advantageous in certain situations to give higher priorities to alternative tasks. In this section we derive an analysis which considers this characteristic. Firstly, we introduce the effects that should be taken into account by the analysis (section 4.1) when alternative tasks execute at a higher priority level. Then, in section 4.2, we derive the equations of the analysis and in section 4.3 some simple but useful properties of the analysis are presented. Finally, using a simple example, we illustrate one of the advantages of using our approach.

div.head: . Simulation Results
div.p: In this section we illustrate, by simulation] the gain in terms of recovery time reduction that can be obtained when alternative tasks are allowed to execute with higher priority. In order to carry out the simulation] random samples of task sets, each one with 10 tasks, were generated. The worst-case computation times of each task set were generated according to an exponential distribution with mean U/10, where U is the generated processor utilization bound. The periods and deadlines of tasks were assigned according to a uniform distribution with minimum and maximum values set to 50 and 5,000, respectively. Deadlines were allowed to be less than or equal to periods. We use the deadline monotonic algorithm to assign the priorities of primary tasks.

We measured the gain of the worst-case recovery time (equation ( 6)) of task 710 (i.e the lowest priority task) considering that its alternative task was executing at 1 levels above 710's priority (1 = 1 , . . . ,9). The choice of the lowest priority task gives us the biggest priority range for the simulation. Certainly some upper priority tasks may miss their deadlines due to the execution interference of 710. Because of this we selected those task sets which are schedulable for 710's priority varying between the lowest and the highest priority. For this simulation 9,600 task sets were selected.2 The task sets were grouped by processor utilization ranges ([0.1-0.2), [0.2-0.3), . . . , [0.8-0.91) so that there were 1,200 tasks sets per range. Then the different recovery time values of 710 executing at priority 10 -1 were compared to the recovery time of 710 executing with the lowest priority.

In order to find an appropriate value of T F , we sought for values of T f considering pr(7lo) = p , for each task set, where p = 1 . . . 1 0 . Then we set TF to the maximum found Tf. This procedure is important since it keeps the same value of TF per task set throughout the simulation, allowing a more accurate comparison.

The procedure to find T f was implemented as a binary search on equation ( 3 ) as (13) suggests. Initially, the interval of search is [mazv, (C,), maxv, ( D z ) ] . This initial interval is appropriate because: (i) TF cannot assume lower values since faults at this rate or higher will continually disrupt the recovery of the tasks; (ii) any larger value for TF will imply only one fault within the maximum response time of any task, i.e. if the task set is not schedulable with TF = m a z v z ( D z ) , this task set will not be schedulable with faults occurring at any rate.

div.head: . Related Work
div.p: Several scheduling mechanisms for fault-tolerant purposes can be found in the literature. Most of them either assume a restrictive task/fault models and so 2Note that a complete evaluation of our approach has to address the problem of choosing alternative task priorities, which is out of the scope of this work. lack flexibility or impose restrictions on the way in which fault tolerance is carried out. Moreover, those approaches, which are briefly described below, assume that alternative tasks run with the same priorities as their respective primaries. Here we refer only to approaches which deal with temporary faults.

In (10) only periodic tasks are considered; the task periods have to be multiple of each other; and the execution times of alternative tasks have to be shorter than the execution times of their respective primaries. The approach presented in (6) considers only reexecution of faulty tasks to tolerate temporary faults. As it is based on the Rate Monotonic priority assignment policy ( l l ) , its disadvantages are inherited by the proposed mechanism. Another approach that uses similar assumptions has been proposed in (a), which carries fault tolerance by periodically checkpointing tasks in different nodes and so both temporary and permanent faults can be tolerated.

In (7) is described a recovery technique that tolerates temporary faults in an off-line scheduled distributed system. It is based on taking advantage of task set spare capacity. The amount of spare capacity is distributed over a given period so that task faults can be handled. Although tasks are assumed to be preemptive and their precedence relations are taken into account, only periodic tasks, whose periods are equal to deadlines, are considered.

An interesting approach to tolerating temporary faults which is independent of the schedulability analysis being used has been described in (5). However, it is considered that recovery is carried out only by re-execution of tasks.

Recently, an EDF based scheduling approach, which takes the effects of temporary faults into account, has been proposed (9). Its basic idea is to simulate the EDF scheduler and to use slack times for executing task recoveries given that a fault pattern or the maximum number of faults per task is known a priory.

A more flexible scheduling was proposed in ( 3 ) . Fault tolerance can be carried out by any error-recovery mechanism since the cost of recovery can be accounted by the schedulability analysis. This approach is represented here by equation (2), which, as we have shown, is a particular case of the analysis we have presented.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this work we have addressed the problem of providing a schedulability analysis for fault-tolerant hard real-time systems regarding temporary faults. We have proposed a suitable solution based on response time analysis that neither impairs the way in which fault tolerance is carried out nor restricts the assumed taskffault models. One important characteristic of our solution is that it allows task recovery to be carried out at higher priority levels. This, as we have seen, has been shown to be a powerful mechanism to increase the flexibility of the analysis, where slack times of higher priority tasks can be better explored. Showing some properties of the analysis, we characterized when it is worth applying our approach.

We have illustrated the advantages of using the described schedulability analyses. By analysing the data collected from simulation we have seen that significant reductions in terms of task recovery time may be obtained by applying the analysis.
Future works will consider heuristics for deciding which higher priority levels to use for general task sets.
